content: Tobramycin is an antibiotic that can cause serious side effects, including hearing loss and kidney damage. Before starting tobramycin, inform your doctor and pharmacist about all prescription and non-prescription medications you are taking, especially diuretics (commonly known as water pills), cisplatin (Platinol), amphotericin (Amphotec, Fungizone), other antibiotics, and vitamins. If you experience symptoms such as dizziness, vertigo, ringing in the ears, hearing loss, numbness, muscle twitching or weakness, difficulty breathing, decreased urination, rash, itching, or a sore throat, contact your healthcare provider immediately. Your doctor has prescribed tobramycin to treat your infection. This medication will either be injected into a large muscle (such as your buttock or hip) or administered intravenously through a needle or catheter placed in your vein. The infusion typically lasts at least 30 minutes and is given one to three times daily. Tobramycin works by eliminating bacteria responsible for various infections, including those affecting the lungs, skin, bones, joints, stomach, blood, and urinary tract. It may also be prescribed for other uses; consult your doctor or pharmacist for additional information. Your healthcare provider will monitor the effectiveness and side effects of your treatment through laboratory tests and physical examinations. It is crucial to attend all scheduled appointments with your doctor and the laboratory. The duration of your treatment will depend on how your infection and symptoms respond to the medication. If you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, inform your doctor. If you become pregnant while taking tobramycin, contact your doctor immediately, as this medication can harm the fetus. Before administering tobramycin, inspect the solution carefully. It should be clear and free of floating particles. Gently squeeze the bag or check the container to ensure there are no leaks. Do not use the solution if it is discolored, contains particles, or if the bag or container is leaking. Use a new solution, but show the damaged one to your healthcare provider. It is essential to use tobramycin exactly as directed. Do not stop your therapy prematurely, as this could worsen your infection and potentially lead to hospitalization. Do not alter your dosing schedule without consulting your healthcare provider. If you encounter a mechanical problem (such as a blockage in the tubing, needle, or catheter) and must stop an infusion, contact your healthcare provider immediately to resume therapy. Tobramycin may cause side effects. To minimize this risk, your healthcare provider may adjust your dose based on blood test results. Follow the instructions in the Important Warning section and report any severe or persistent symptoms to your healthcare provider. Common side effects include upset stomach, vomiting, fatigue, and pale skin. If you experience severe rash or difficulty breathing, contact your doctor immediately. Serious side effects can be reported to the FDA's MedWatch Adverse Event Reporting program online or by phone. If you are receiving tobramycin intravenously, you will likely be instructed to store it in the refrigerator or freezer. Take your next dose out of the refrigerator one hour before use and place it in a clean, dry area to allow it to warm to room temperature. If additional tobramycin is stored in the freezer, move a 24-hour supply to the refrigerator for the next day's use. Do not refreeze medications. If you are receiving tobramycin intramuscularly, your healthcare provider will provide specific storage instructions. Store your medication only as directed and ensure you understand proper storage procedures. Keep all medications and supplies in a clean, dry place and out of reach of children. Your healthcare provider will instruct you on how to safely dispose of used needles, syringes, tubing, and containers to prevent accidental injury. In case of an overdose, contact your local poison control center at 1-800-222-1222. If the individual collapses or is not breathing, call emergency services at 911. If you are receiving tobramycin intravenously or under your skin, be aware of the symptoms of a catheter-related infection, which occurs where the needle enters your vein or skin.
